items.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
items.independence: Independently read the archived official PDF, including Sections 4.1 and 5.1, Appendix C.2, the ablation table and Appendix F. Root and source agent supplied the proposed narrow branch; it was checked against primary text and future-work counterevidence.
items.review_scope: Official identity/date/abstract matching and source-bound review of the pre-task executable skill-building loop, reuse, ablation scope and future-work limitation. No code execution, empirical reproduction or full-paper numerical recalculation.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 6; Section 4.1, Action interface with receipts
summary_source_claims.quote: Action interface with receipts. The agent acts through a three-layer API. Shared entry points for grasping, placing, corrective motions, reachability checks, and coordinated bimanual motion are environment-independent. An environment binding discovered by automated probes supplies coordinate frames, joint limits, table height, and gripper characteristics. Before learning, the agent builds environment-specific skills on these two layers. It segments each demonstration into action primitives, identifies which segments the existing entries cannot explain, and hands each gap to a coding agent that writes a skill. A driver validates each skill by running it on the demonstration scene and checking that it transfers to other layouts without encoding any absolute position. The loop repeats until coverage stops improving, and the final skill set is frozen before task learning.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 17; Appendix C.1, Shared and environment-specific skills
summary_source_claims.quote: Shared and environment-specific skills. Skills are divided by whether they depend on the environment. Shared entry points cover common operations such as observing, grasping, placing, corrective motions, reachability checks, arm selection, and coordinated bimanual motion. These entry points hold no convention of any environment. Environment conventions, including coordinate frames, end-effector-to-fingertip offsets, gripper normalization, the collision world, and arm names, enter the shared entry points as data through a binding. An operation that holds only in a particular environment is an environment-specific skill, and it becomes visible only when that environment is loaded.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 17; Appendix C.2, Coverage of the demonstrations
summary_source_claims.quote: Coverage of the demonstrations. Skill building starts from the demonstrations of all tasks. Each demonstration is cut at its gripper events into segments of seven kinds, namely grasp, place, carry, touch, release, move, and return home. A segment is explained when an existing entry point or written skill, with parameters fitted to the demonstration, reproduces it from the state where the segment starts. Each task is checked in two ways. Every segment is replayed from its own start, and the plan of the whole task is also rolled out once from the reset, so that each call starts where the previous calls left the scene. Segments that no entry explains are gaps, and gaps of the same kind and failure class are grouped into clusters.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 17; Appendix C.2, Written skills
summary_source_claims.quote: Written skills. Each cluster is handed to a coding agent that works in a sandbox with fixed budgets of case runs, wall-clock time, and tokens. A written skill has two parts. The action part runs at the deployable tier, exactly as the agent runs it in rehearsal and deployment, and it uses only the action API, the object handles it receives, and its parameters. The fitting part runs only during skill building and may read the recording and the ground-truth scene. It returns the parameters that reproduce one segment. These parameters hold no absolute position, since the fit is repeated on the demonstration moved across the table and a parameter that moves with it by more than 1 cm rejects the fit.

Gate. The driver accepts a skill only through its own checks and never relies on the report of the coding agent. A static check rejects imports outside an allowed set, task names, object labels, and position literals. The skill must then explain the gaps it was written for. A transfer check runs its fitted parameters on the same segment of up to three other demonstrations whose object lies at least 5 cm away, and rejects a skill that explains none of them, so that a replay cannot pass as a skill. Finally, all sweeps of the round run again with the accepted skills and the candidates, and a candidate is dropped when its confirmed losses outweigh its gains. Every process that imports a written skill runs in the sandbox.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 18; Appendix C.2, Stopping and freezing
summary_source_claims.quote: Stopping and freezing. Rounds repeat until coverage stops growing, measured by explained segments, task rollouts that reach the end, official successes of the rolled-out plans, and completed stages. The accepted skills are then frozen as the skill set of the environment. The task plans that the builder uses to measure coverage stay in its records and never enter the skill set, a Task Memory, or any input of learning or deployment.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 8; Section 5.1, Benchmark and protocol
summary_source_claims.quote: Benchmark and protocol. RoboTwin 2.0 [11] defines 50 dual-arm tasks in a clean setting (fixed background) and a randomized setting (randomized textures, lighting, table height, and distractors). The agent first builds its skill set across all 50 tasks, then learns each task from one automatically selected clean demonstration, with rehearsal on clean scenes only. The frozen Task Memory is evaluated in both settings with the official server, unseen instructions, and the official step limit. Each task is evaluated on 10 episodes per setting (1,000 episodes total), as each episode requires dozens of model calls. We report success rate averaged over all tasks, the mean of the two settings, and retention (randomized divided by clean).

Baselines. Trained action policies (VLAs and WAMs) are trained on all 50 tasks with 50 clean demonstrations per task and evaluated on 100 episodes. The agent-with-policy baseline is HarnessVLA [93], which orchestrates a fine-tuned VLA with a coding agent. All baseline results come from the official leaderboard [11] or published reports, excluding policies trained on randomized data.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 10; Section 5.4, Where Do the Gains Come From?
summary_source_claims.quote: Tab. 2 removes one component at a time. Deployment ablations use the frozen memory from the main run, the second group builds a memory without interacting with the world, and learning ablations relearn every memory from scratch. All groups use the same 10 tasks covering all five categories, with 10 episodes per task in each setting on shared seeds, so all comparisons are paired and we report exact McNemar p values.

summary_source_claims.locator: PDF page 24; Appendix F, Future work
summary_source_claims.quote: Future work. Beyond these limitations, the agentic side of WICL remains largely unexplored. Agents could build new skills when existing ones fail, coordinate several specialized agents over a long task, or rehearse in learned world models when no simulator is available. Our results also suggest that agent-centric embodied models are a promising direction. A foundation model trained to use embodied tools, read physical feedback, and maintain a task memory could make WICL faster, cheaper, and more reliable than general-purpose models accessed through an API.

summary_override.summary_zh: RoboScript 在任务学习前把汇集的示范拆为动作片段，将现有接口无法覆盖的缺口交给 coding agent 编写环境技能。独立 driver 回放、检查跨布局复用并复查新增技能的得失，按覆盖反馈迭代后冻结技能库，供后续任务调用。这里仅将可执行工具技能的构建与筛选闭环纳入 Harness；普通 Task Memory 内容更新另计。论文未单独量化技能构建的贡献，部署中遇到失败再持续生成新技能仍是未来工作。
summary_override.summary_en: Before task learning, RoboScript segments the collected demonstrations and asks a coding agent to write environment-specific skills for gaps in the existing action interface. An independent driver replays the skills, checks transfer across layouts, and rechecks gains against regressions. Coverage feedback drives further rounds before the skill library is frozen for later tasks. Inclusion is limited to this executable tool-skill construction and selection loop, separate from ordinary Task Memory content updates. The paper does not isolate the contribution of skill construction, and continual failure-driven skill creation during deployment remains future work.

items.summary_en: Before task learning, RoboScript segments the collected demonstrations and asks a coding agent to write environment-specific skills for gaps in the existing action interface. An independent driver replays the skills, checks transfer across layouts, and rechecks gains against regressions. Coverage feedback drives further rounds before the skill library is frozen for later tasks. Inclusion is limited to this executable tool-skill construction and selection loop, separate from ordinary Task Memory content updates. The paper does not isolate the contribution of skill construction, and continual failure-driven skill creation during deployment remains future work.
limits: Only the pre-task executable skill-building branch is used for Harness inclusion; ordinary Task Memory or reflection-content edits are separate.
The implemented skill set is frozen before task learning. Continually building new skills after later failures is listed as future work, not established deployment behavior.
Skill construction uses demonstrations across the benchmark tasks; this is not unseen-task-family transfer.
Skill fitting may use recorded ground-truth data during construction, while the action half uses deployable tools. This is not a claim of wholly unprivileged construction.
The reported main results evaluate the combined system. Table 2 does not isolate the effect of the skill-building loop.
Baseline numbers come from leaderboards or published reports rather than all being rerun under matched budgets.
No implementation execution, code-artifact audit or independent empirical validation was performed for this review.
